name: J. Howard Pew

summary.text: J. Howard Pew (1882–1971) became president of the Sun Oil Company on his father's death in 1912 and held the post until 1947. In 1948 he and his siblings co-founded what became The Pew Charitable Trusts. The Philanthropy Roundtable describes his giving as directed to the Presbyterian Church, higher education and free-enterprise principles. Historian Kevin Kruse identifies him as the main sponsor of James Fifield's Spiritual Mobilization; he contributed $150,000 to launch Christianity Today in 1956 and was instrumental in the Christian Freedom Foundation, which sent its Christian Economics newsletter to about 180,000 ministers.

facts.claim: Pew became president of the Sun Oil Company when his father died in 1912 and held the position until 1947.
facts.quote: When his father died in 1912, he became president of the Sun Oil Company a position he was to hold until 1947.

facts.claim: In 1948 Pew and his siblings co-founded The Pew Charitable Trusts; the Trusts' own history says its funding comes from seven charitable funds set up between 1948 and 1979 by the four children of Sun Oil founder Joseph Newton Pew.
facts.quote: In 1948, Pew and his siblings co-founded The Pew Charitable Trusts, a non-profit, non-governmental organization with the purpose of serving the public.

facts.claim: Historian Kevin Kruse, in One Nation Under God (2015), describes James Fifield as a front man for corporate leaders and names Pew as the main sponsor of Spiritual Mobilization, with Alfred Sloan of General Motors and the heads of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers among its other funders.
facts.quote: Its funders included Sun Oil President J. Howard Pew, Alfred Sloan of General Motors, the heads of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the National Association of Manufacturers

sources.title: How 'One Nation' Didn't Become 'Under God' Until The '50s Religious Revival

facts.claim: The Philanthropy Roundtable says Pew contributed $150,000 to launch Carl Henry's Christianity Today magazine in 1956 and provided most of the funds to send it free to nearly every member of the Christian clergy in North America.
facts.quote: contributed $150,000 to launch Carl Henry's Christianity Today magazine in 1956

facts.claim: The Philanthropy Roundtable says Pew was instrumental in the Christian Freedom Foundation, which distributed a 'Christian Economics' newsletter to about 180,000 ministers, and that he also supported the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, the National Association of Evangelicals and the International Congress on World Evangelization.
facts.quote: instrumental in the Christian Freedom Foundation, which distributed a "Christian Economics" newsletter to about 180,000 ministers

facts.claim: Christianity Today's 1971 obituary editorial credits Pew as one of the founders of the Presbyterian Lay Committee; the Philanthropy Roundtable says he chaired the National Lay Committee and was president of the board of trustees.
facts.quote: one of the founders of the Presbyterian Lay Committee

facts.claim: Pew joined the board of Grove City College in 1912 and served until his death, including four decades as chairman.

openQuestions: Site claim (Kruse: Pew bankrolled Fifield's Spiritual Mobilization) is supported by Kruse's NPR interview and The Nation; dollar amounts of Pew's gifts to Spiritual Mobilization were not found in any opened source.

Pew is listed as an early contributor to the Foundation for Economic Education only in a tertiary summary; the amount and date need a primary source (FEE's own histories name Volker/Luhnow and DuPont's Jasper Crane, not Pew).

Is there a Pew Charitable Trusts page that itself records the Christianity Today or Christian Freedom Foundation grants? The Trusts' history page describes early grants as anonymous and names cancer research, the Red Cross and historically black colleges as early priorities.
